title: The Doctor China Remembered
shortDescription: A doctor from a middle-class family in Solapur who sailed to China in 1938 with a five-man medical mission, operated for the Communist Eighth Route Army, married a Chinese nurse and died at thirty-two. China built him memorials, printed his face on stamps and still brings leaders to his family's door. In India, his own country, he is almost unknown.
introduction: Tang County, in the northern Chinese province of Hebei, December 1942. A thirty-two-year-old Indian doctor lay dying in a village clinic after four years of surgery in a war that was not his own. Within a generation a Chinese city would build him a memorial, and India would print his face on a stamp. Yet in the country of his birth his name barely registers. Dwarkanath Shantaram Kotnis was not a destitute boy who conquered an empire, and he never commanded an army. He was a doctor from a modest family in Solapur who answered a call, crossed the sea, and became the rarest thing in either country: a man whom each remembers differently.

chapters.heading: Solapur
paragraphs: Dwarkanath Shantaram Kotnis was born on 10 October 1910 in Sholapur, as Solapur was then spelled, in the Bombay Presidency of British India. His father, Shantaram Narayan Kotnis, worked in the textile mills and held a public role in the municipality; accounts disagree on whether he was a clerk, a mill manager or a municipal official. The family was comfortably known in the town, not poor. Indian government features call it a middle-class Maharashtrian family, and the schoolbooks that call it lower-middle-class do not cite their evidence. There were several children, commonly given as seven, though the surviving lists do not agree on their names.

Solapur had known plague, and a surgeon and medical historian writing in Mumbai in 2020 noted that the family moved out of the city during an outbreak. He was careful about what this meant: it seems, he wrote, that the childhood experience inspired the choice of medicine. That is an inference, not a documented decision, and it belongs in the story only with the uncertainty attached. The more dramatic version, in which the boy inoculates himself with plague in a fit of scientific daring, is a scene from a 1946 film about him, not an event from his life.

Schooling is another small fog. A family exhibition in Mumbai named a school in Vengurla; Chinese-language biographies name Northcote High School in Solapur and Deccan College in Pune. What is firmer is the medical education. He entered Seth G. S. Medical College in Bombay, a college founded in 1926 by Indian nationalists as an answer to the British-run Grant Medical College, and was caught in a student strike there. He was told to leave and continue at Grant. In 2011 researchers found his old career card at Grant Medical College, recording internships in vaccination and in winter and summer infections. He qualified as a doctor in 1936. Short official biographies collapse the two colleges into one; the record shows he attended both.

His family wanted him to marry, settle in Solapur and practise near home. He wanted surgery, and he wanted to travel. His sister Manorama remembered that nobody in the family knew much about China in those years. They knew it, she said, because men came to the door selling Chinese silk. That was the whole of his country's knowledge of the place he would make his home for the last four years of his life. He asked his family's permission to go. It was granted.

media.alt: A black-and-white portrait of Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis photographed in China in the 1940s
media.caption: Kotnis in China in the 1940s. The photograph survived in Chinese archives and returned to India through the families and institutions that kept his memory alive; almost no image of him as a doctor in India circulates today.

chapters.heading: The call
paragraphs: In 1937 Japan invaded China, and the war that followed killed millions. China's Nationalists and Communists had formed a united front against the invader, and the Communists' fighting arm was called the Eighth Route Army. The Chinese commander Zhu De wrote to Jawaharlal Nehru asking for doctors. Some accounts add the name of the American journalist Agnes Smedley as the person who first suggested the appeal; that detail is repeated often but rests on thinner sourcing than the letter itself. Nehru took the request to the Indian National Congress, which created a committee to raise money and choose a team.

Subhas Chandra Bose, as Congress president, issued a press statement on 30 June 1938. He declared an All-India China Day, fixed fund-raising days for early July, and said an ambulance had been ordered from Ford's to be sent straight to Hong Kong. The Congress's fifty-second session passed the resolution. More than seven hundred people answered the call, among them about a hundred doctors. The committee picked five: Madan Mohan Lal Atal of Allahabad, a veteran of medical aid in the Spanish Civil War, who led the team; M. R. Cholkar of Nagpur; Bejoy Kumar Basu and Debesh Mukherjee of Calcutta; and Kotnis from Sholapur. A doctor named Ranen Sen was first selected but refused permission by the British because he was a communist, and he suggested Basu in his place. The process was a committee's, not a personal choice by Nehru, though retellings often make it one.

On 31 August 1938 a public meeting at Jinnah Hall in Bombay said goodbye to the five. Sarojini Naidu, the poet and independence leader who chaired it, fastened Red Cross bands on their arms and warned them that some, or one of them, might not come back. Kotnis was twenty-seven, a month from twenty-eight. The next morning they sailed from Ballard Pier on the SS Rajputana. Basu's diary remembers him so heavily garlanded that nothing showed except his weary, exultant face. The ship called at Colombo, Penang, Singapore and Hong Kong. The party reached Chinese soil at Guangzhou on 17 September, according to Basu's diary and Chinese records; an Indian government account says their first arrival was at Hankou, in Wuhan. Both cannot be the first. They moved on through Changsha and Hankou, worked with the Chinese Red Cross, went west to Yichang and Chongqing, and reached Yan'an on 12 February 1939.

chapters.heading: Yan'an
paragraphs: Yan'an, in the northern province of Shaanxi, was the wartime capital of the Chinese Communists: a cave-city of party offices, schools and hospitals from which the Eighth Route Army directed the war behind Japanese lines. To an Indian doctor who had known only silk merchants, it was another planet. Kotnis arrived in February 1939 and met Mao Zedong the following month. In July he treated Zhou Enlai, later China's premier, after a fall from a horse. The details come from an Indian think-tank's reconstruction of the mission and from Chinese official accounts, and they should be read as such; the period documents that survive are mostly letters and diaries rather than medical case notes. He also acquired a Chinese name, Ke Dihua, a phonetic rendering of Kotnis that Chinese-language sources date to December 1938, though Indian records do not confirm the day. It is the name carved on the memorials and written in the hospital registers; the English one is the name on the Indian stamp.

In November 1939 he left Yan'an for Wuxiang, headquarters of the Eighth Route Army, and then for the border region the Chinese call Jin-Cha-Ji, where the provinces of Shanxi, Chahar and Hebei meet. This was guerrilla country: villages, mountain tracks and field hospitals that moved when the army moved. Surgery there meant wounds, infection and amputations done with whatever equipment could be carried. Kotnis also taught, and he began writing surgical textbooks for Chinese students who had almost nothing to learn from.

Of the five who had sailed together, some went home. Cholkar returned in May 1939; Mukherjee left the same year after falling ill. Nehru wrote in April 1939 that the mission was likely to remain in China for at least another year, and that Atal and Basu had offered to stay as long as the Chinese wanted them. Kotnis was not named in that appeal, but he stayed the longest. He was one of very few foreigners inside the Communist base area, and movement in and out of it was slow and dangerous once the war settled into its long middle years. The mission had been planned as a year's service. It became the rest of his life.

chapters.heading: The hospital in the mountains
paragraphs: The most famous Canadian in wartime China was Norman Bethune, a surgeon who had established medical services for the Eighth Route Army and died of blood poisoning from an operation on 12 November 1939. Chinese commemorations often place Kotnis at Bethune's side. The chronology does not support a meeting: Kotnis reached Yan'an three months after Bethune's death, and the Jin-Cha-Ji base area later still. What can be said is that he laid a wreath at Bethune's tomb, that Chinese accounts describe him swearing by it, and that he was deliberately cast as Bethune's successor. In 1941 he became director of the Bethune International Peace Hospital. He taught at the Bethune Hygiene School and worked on surgical manuals. The hospital and the school carry the Canadian's name; the Indian doctor inherited both.

Then there are the numbers. Chinese state media and Indian retellings say that during one battle he operated for up to seventy-two hours without sleep and treated more than eight hundred wounded in thirteen days. Other versions give 558 operations in the Laishui campaign, or 580, or 430 including forty-five amputations. No independent record settles any of these figures. They come from a tradition of praise, and the tradition inflates. The honest sentence is that he performed a great deal of surgery under conditions that would stop most trained surgeons today, and that the exact counts are not known. A claim about plague-control work, including testing a vaccine on himself, appears in one Indian newspaper report in 2012 and has not been independently confirmed.

What survives without exaggeration is quieter. He kept operating in field hospitals. He taught nurses and doctors in a language he had to learn. He wrote textbooks because the surgeons coming after him would have no one else to teach them. A letter of his from April 1942, preserved in a collection built from more than seventy of his letters, tells a friend in India that he considers 1941 one of the most important years of his life. He does not say why in the passage usually quoted. He does not need to.

media.alt: An old black-and-white photograph of Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis laying a wreath at a memorial to Dr. Norman Bethune
media.caption: Kotnis laying a wreath in memory of Norman Bethune, the Canadian surgeon whose work with the Eighth Route Army he carried on. Chinese commemorations treat the two men as a line of succession; the record does not show that they ever met.
media.credit: Unknown photographer, reproduced on Wikimedia Commons — Public domain (China)

chapters.heading: Yinhua
paragraphs: In November or December 1941, at the Bethune International Peace Hospital, Kotnis married Guo Qinglan, a Chinese nurse who worked there. The month varies between Indian and Chinese accounts; the marriage does not. The hospital had been named for a Canadian surgeon who died in 1939, so the wedding took place inside a building that was already a memorial to another foreign doctor. She was known in later life as Guo Qinglan Kotnis. When a 2012 report in The Hindu recorded her death in Dalian in 2011 at the age of ninety-six, it noted that she had remarried but had kept her first husband's name. Chinese leaders visiting India would ask after her.

Their son was born on 23 August 1942. At the suggestion of Nie Rongzhen, a senior Communist commander, they named him Yinhua. The first character, yin, is the short form of Yin-du, India; the second, hua, is China. Chinese-language records give the boy's full name as Ke Yinhua, using the surname his father had taken. The name was a small act of double belonging, given in a wartime hospital in northern China to a child whose father would not live to see him grow up. It is the most precise thing anyone ever said about this life, and it needs no speech to explain it.

The boy died in 1967. Whether he was twenty-four or twenty-five, and whether the cause was a medical error or gastroenteritis, are both disputed in the sources that mention him. Guo Qinglan outlived him by more than four decades. By keeping the name, she remained in the records of her own country for the rest of her life the widow of an Indian doctor who had died in a war between China and Japan. The family story ends in ordinary grief rather than in the symbolism that later writers tried to give it.

chapters.heading: The last page
paragraphs: Kotnis had epilepsy. It was known to him and kept quiet, and the strain of the work made it worse. Accounts written after his death say he had kept the condition private even from colleagues, and that exhaustion made the seizures more frequent. The order of those events is not firmly documented, but the secrecy and the decline are repeated in both Indian and Chinese accounts. He died on 9 December 1942, aged thirty-two. Where he died is genuinely uncertain: Chinese and Indian sources variously name a village in Tang County rendered as Kokun, Gegong or Nanquan, a hospital in Baoding, and Shijiazhuang, which is certainly where his remains were later laid in the North China Martyrs' Cemetery. The constant is the date and the age. The place has been smoothed over by commemoration, as if a hero ought to die in a named building rather than in a village whose name no two accounts spell alike.

One Chinese account says he collapsed on 8 December while writing page 173 of a second surgery textbook. Another gives page 177, and gives different operation totals for the same period. The figure of a surgeon dying over a manual he was writing for his students is vivid enough that both traditions want it. It may even be true. But a story that cares about the truth has to say that the page number is not settled, and leave the image with its edge intact.

The 1946 Indian film about him, Dr. Kotnis Ki Amar Kahani, showed a young man who overcame a cruel world through courage and science. The real man had a quieter start, a committee's selection, a public farewell and a family's permission. He was not a saint who never doubted and he was not a poor boy from a village of legends. He was a working doctor who kept going until his body stopped.

media.alt: The tomb of Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis in the North China Martyrs' Cemetery in Shijiazhuang, Hebei province
media.caption: His Chinese-style tomb in the North China Martyrs' Cemetery at Shijiazhuang. His remains were brought here after his death in 1942; the cemetery holds the martyrs of the wars China fought in the twentieth century.

chapters.heading: A hero in two countries
paragraphs: V. Shantaram's 1946 film Dr. Kotnis Ki Amar Kahani, written by K. A. Abbas and V. P. Sathe from Abbas's piece And One Did Not Come Back, made Kotnis a household name in India for a time. China made its own film, Ke Di Hua Dai Fu, in 1982. China issued stamps bearing his face in 1982 and 1992; India followed with a commemorative stamp on 9 December 1993. A Mao Zedong tribute is reproduced on memorials and in almost every account, but the BBC, reporting from India and China in 2013, called the attribution reported rather than verified. In 2009 a Chinese internet poll named him among the ten foreign friends who had done most for China in a century. Chinese leaders have called on his family in India for decades, a ritual of a friendship that predates the border war of 1962.

The physical record is easier to verify. There is a memorial to him in Shijiazhuang and a memorial hall in Tang County. A hall at the Bethune International Peace Hospital carries his name, as does the Kotnis India-China Friendship Hospital at Hebei Medical University. In Solapur, a memorial hospital opened in 1976 and his former residence became a memorial in 2012. New exhibition halls opened in Hebei in December 2025. Official Chinese media call him Dr Thoughtful and Old Ke, names of affection rather than ceremony. An Indian historian, Vinay Lal, described the contrast in one sentence: adulation, even veneration, in China; largely forgotten in India.

The BBC put it more plainly in 2013. At home, it wrote, Dr Kotnis appears to be a little-known figure these days. In China he is revered as a hero. The generation that saw the 1946 film has passed, and the other four doctors of the mission have faded from memory too. The 1962 war between the two countries settled over the story like dust. What remains is a name on a hospital in Hebei, a name on a street in Solapur, a stamp in an album, and a son's two-character name that joins the two countries more neatly than any treaty.

media.alt: A memorial statue of Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis at the North China Martyrs' Cemetery in Shijiazhuang
media.caption: The memorial statue at Shijiazhuang. Kotnis is one of the few foreigners honoured in a Chinese cemetery of revolutionary martyrs, and Chinese officials still lay wreaths here on the anniversary of his death.

chapters.heading: What the record keeps
paragraphs: A truth-first account of this life has to refuse most of the colour that has been poured over it. He was not poor. His father was a mill worker and municipal figure with a position in Solapur, and the poverty-stricken childhood of the film is the film's invention. He did not inject himself with plague. Nehru did not pluck him from a crowd; a committee interviewed hundreds of volunteers. He did not leave in secret; a public meeting and a crowd at Ballard Pier sent him off. He probably did not operate for seventy-two consecutive hours, and nobody can say how many patients he treated in thirteen days. None of this makes the life smaller. It makes it possible to believe.

The facts that remain are sufficient. A young Indian doctor with a taste for travel and surgery took a ship to a country he knew through silk salesmen. He learned its language, worked in hospitals that moved with an army, taught its students from books he wrote himself, married one of its nurses and gave his son a name made of both countries. He died at thirty-two and was buried among China's martyrs. India printed his face on a stamp two decades later and then mostly forgot him.

There is a lesson here, though it is not the one the films tell. A country's record is not the same as a life, and a life can be kept more faithfully by the people it touched than by the monuments raised to it. China kept Kotnis because he served its people in their worst year. India let him go because the story of the man who went away did not fit the story it wanted to tell about itself. The photograph on this page came back from China. That is where his memory survived, and that is where a reader has to go to find him.

media.alt: The 1993 Indian postage stamp commemorating Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis, showing his portrait
media.caption: India Post issued this stamp on 9 December 1993, fifty-one years after his death. It is the clearest sign that the country which sent him had begun, however briefly, to remember him too.
media.credit: India Post, Government of India — GODL-India

sources.title: Jawaharlal Nehru, 'Medical Mission to China', 8 April 1939, Selected Works, First Series, Vol. 9, p. 250
sources.note: Primary text. Nehru's appeal for the mission, its intended duration, the readiness of Atal and Basu to stay on, and the footnote recording Kotnis's departure for China on 1 September 1938 and the early return of Cholkar and Mukherjee.

sources.title: 'The Indian doctors who risked their lives to support China in its war with Japan'
sources.publisher: Scroll.in (based on Bejoy Kumar Basu's diaries)
sources.note: Strongest sourcing for the selection committee, the five doctors, Ranen Sen's exclusion and Basu's substitution, the Jinnah Hall farewell, Naidu's warning, the SS Rajputana departure, the garland quote, and the route through Guangzhou, Changsha, Hankou, Yichang and Chongqing.

sources.title: 'An Indian doctor in China', Mumbai Mirror opinion column by Sanjay Nagral
sources.note: Surgeon-historian on the hedged plague episode, the two medical colleges and the student strike, the SS Rajputana, and the family's wish that he settle in Solapur. The plague-to-medicine link is explicitly speculative in the original.

sources.title: 'Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis' feature and biography
sources.publisher: Embassy of India, Belgrade / Press Information Bureau, Government of India
sources.note: Indian government account: 10 October 1910 birth, middle-class Solapur family, the five mission doctors, the desire to travel, the family's permission, the 1946 film and the Indian stamp. Its claim that the party first arrived at Hankou conflicts with the diary-based Guangzhou route.

sources.title: 'Why is India's Dr Kotnis revered in China?'
sources.note: Independent press. Source for the revered-in-China / little-known-in-India contrast, the 2009 Chinese internet poll, Chinese leaders visiting the family, and the deliberate hedge that Mao's tribute is only 'reportedly' attributed. Also confirms the marriage to Guo Qinglan.

sources.title: 'Framing discourse on China in the modern world'
sources.publisher: UCLA South Asia / Economic & Political Weekly (Vinay Lal)
sources.note: Academic framing of Kotnis as a symbol of pre-1962 India-China anti-imperial solidarity, and of the asymmetry between adulation in China and being largely forgotten in India.

sources.title: 'The undying influence and memory of Dr Kotnis'
sources.note: Indian think-tank reconstruction drawing on Chinese and Indian sources. Used for the detailed itinerary (Yan'an February 1939, meeting with Mao in March, Zhou Enlai's fall in July, Wuxiang and Jin-Cha-Ji), the son's name Yinhua, and the 558-operation variant of the Laishui figures.

sources.title: 'Doctor's inspiring legacy given a fresh take'
sources.note: Chinese state media, read as the official commemorative narrative rather than as independent verification. Source for the seventy-two-hour and 800-patient claim, the 1941 hospital directorship, and the collapse while writing a surgery textbook. Its figures conflict with other official versions.

sources.title: 'Wife of Dwarkanath Kotnis is no more'
sources.note: Guo Qinglan's death in Dalian in 2011 at the age of ninety-six, her retained married name, the known epilepsy, and the single-source plague-vaccine claim, which the story hedges rather than asserts.

sources.title: 'When Subhas Chandra Bose sent the Indian Medical Mission to China against Japan'
sources.note: Reproduces Bose's 30 June 1938 press statement in full: All-India China Day, fund days, the ordered ambulance, and the Congress mechanism. Also the origin of Ranen Sen's selection and his substitution of Basu.

sources.title: 'Remembering Dr Kotnis', by M. Bapuji
sources.note: Compilation citing Basu 1982 and a Chinese book based on more than seventy Kotnis letters. Used for the letter of April 1942, the wreath at Bethune's tomb, Naidu's alternative wording, and the conflicting textbook page number. Ideological framing; factual claims cross-checked elsewhere.

sources.title: 'Researchers discover Kotnis's career card in Mumbai'
sources.note: Physical evidence from Grant Medical College for the vaccination and infection internships, supporting the two-college sequence over the shortened official biographies.

sources.title: 'Dr. Kotnis Ki Amar Kahani' (1946), film catalogue entry
sources.note: Credits for V. Shantaram's film: directors and writers K. A. Abbas and V. P. Sathe, and its basis in Abbas's 'And One Did Not Come Back'. Distinguishes the film's dramatised episodes from the life.

sources.title: 'In Memory of Norman Bethune', Mao Zedong
sources.publisher: Marxists.org, Selected Works of Mao Tse-tung, Vol. II
sources.note: Primary text establishing Bethune's death on 12 November 1939 from blood poisoning contracted while operating. The chronology rules out a personal meeting between Bethune and Kotnis.

sources.title: 'Where China remembers India's wartime doctors'
sources.note: Independent treatment of the memory asymmetry: the generation that saw the 1946 film has gone, the other mission doctors have faded, and the 1962 war changed how India tells the story.

sources.title: 'Indian doctor China remembers as a hero who was Dr Dwarkanath Kotnis'
sources.note: Reporting on the December 2025 opening of new memorial exhibition halls in Hebei, and on the present state of the Chinese memorials.
